title: Troy VI: the Citadel as the Spade Found It

sources.cite: Dörpfeld, Wilhelm. Troja und Ilion: Ergebnisse der Ausgrabungen in den vorhistorischen und historischen Schichten von Ilion, 1870–1894. 2 vols. Athens: Beck & Barth, 1902. Tafel V, “Troja VI, die Burg der mykenischen Zeit, das Troja Homers”, 1:800.

layers.note: The west wall, from the point in the north-west where the circuit simply stops to the West Gate VI U. This is the rougher, older work of the ring — unwrought stone, where the south and east stretches are cut ashlar — and Dörpfeld took those finer stretches for a rebuilding within the life of Troy VI, which is why the circuit reads as two buildings joined. The line is a polygon and not a curve: “im Äusseren sehen wir die Linie der Mauer als Polygon aus geraden Stücken von fast gleicher Länge gebildet” (Dörpfeld 1902, 2:611) — straight lengths of nearly equal size, each set a little forward of the last, so the wall turns the hill in steps and never has to make a corner, a corner being the weak point of a defence. Every offset drawn here is one he surveyed. House VI A stands hard against the inner face along this stretch and is drawn with the wall, because it is drawn with the wall on his plate. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.note: The south wall, from the West Gate VI U to the South Gate VI T, ending in the south tower VI i. Measured across the drawn band the masonry runs 4.4 to 5.3 m thick along here. Dörpfeld printed the wall in two tones and said why: “bei der Festungsmauer ist der Unterbau hellrot, die dünnere Obermauer dunkelrot getönt” (1902, 2:650) — the substructure light red, the thinner upper wall dark red. This plate draws the two together, as one footprint, because that is what a reader standing outside the wall would have seen: one face. Homer's Trojans have their wall from a god. Poseidon made it πόλιν πέρι τεῖχος ... εὐρύ τε καὶ μάλα καλόν, wide and very beautiful, that the city might be unbreakable (Il. 21.446-47), and resents that men will remember the Achaeans' wall and forget the one he and Apollo built for Laomedon (7.452-53). Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it. How the sheet was made: Tafel V, drawn at 1:800, was rectified on its own printed 20 m grid — ninety-nine grid intersections recovered by line-fitting, a projective transform fitted through them, mean residual 0.15 m of ground and worst 0.5 m, finer than the drawn line itself. The squares check against Dörpfeld's own text: the shaft wells he places in J 4 and K 4 fall in squares J 4 and K 4 here. Everything on this sheet is therefore his survey at one uniform scale, 218 m of ground east to west by 158 m north to south. It is oriented as he printed it — “der Plan ist nach der magnetischen Nordlinie orientirt”, to the magnetic north line of the 1890s and not to true north — and no rotation has been applied. The modern excavation net kept his 20 m grid and tied it to a world coordinate system by GPS in 2000 (Messmer 2014), so this plan can be put on the ground; the plate does not do it, because a citadel plan wants the wall, not a latitude.

layers.note: The south-east and east wall, from the South Gate VI T to the East Gate VI S, with the great tower VI h jutting from it. This is the finest masonry on the site: rectangular limestone laid without mortar, the face battered so that it leans back as it rises, and stepped forward every few metres in the offsets this trace keeps. The tower stands midway between the two gates — “der Turm VI h liegt in der Mitte zwischen den zwei Thoren VI S und VI T” (Dörpfeld 1902, 1:121 ff.) — which is where a tower belongs, at the point where the wall face has to be swept from the flank. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.note: The north-east stretch: the outer arm of the East Gate, run out beyond the circuit and overlapping it, and the wall running north from it toward the great tower. The overlap is the most sophisticated piece of military architecture on the hill. It turns the approach to the East Gate into a blind corridor, so that the door cannot be seen from outside and cannot be come at head-on — a ram cannot be brought to a gate it cannot see. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.label: Tower VI g
layers.note: Tower VI g, the largest on the circuit, drawn with the surviving north-east end of the wall that carries it. Tolman and Scoggin, following Dörpfeld, give it 18 m broad and projecting 8 m, “the most stately tower”; inside it a shaft sunk to water gave the citadel its supply under cover. North of this the circuit stops. Dörpfeld notes independently that a shaft well of Troy VI, his B b, lies in square K 4 — which is this tower. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.label: VI R
layers.note: VI R: the northernmost piece of Troy VI masonry left on the hill, curving away beyond the great tower, outside the line of the citadel wall. Dörpfeld locates it in square K 3. It is the last thing the spade found in this direction; everything north and west of it was cut away for the precinct of Athena. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.label: VI M
layers.note: House VI M, about 29 by 21 m over all — the largest single building left standing inside the circuit — set on its own terrace above the south wall, with open ground between it and the ring. Homer gives Priam a palace of polished stone with fifty chambers for his sons and twelve more across the court for his daughters' husbands (Il. 6.242-50). The largest hall the spade has found inside this wall would stand inside one wing of that. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.label: VI b
layers.note: House VI b, in the north-west of the citadel, on the highest ground where anything of Troy VI still stood when Dörpfeld dug. What is drawn is what survived: arms of walling, cut off where the levelling for the Athena precinct began. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.label: VI C
layers.note: The block of the east terrace — Dörpfeld's houses VI D, VI C, VI E and VI F, drawn together because they are drawn together, wall against wall, on his sheet. VI C is the hall in the middle of the block. The citadel was built as terraces rising toward the centre, each held up by a retaining wall with the houses standing on the level ground behind, and this is the second of them. The double circles Dörpfeld draws inside these rooms are pithoi, storage jars sunk in the floors (1902, 2:649). Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.note: House VI Q, the north-easternmost of the terrace houses to survive. Immediately north of it the Hellenistic and Roman cutting for the temple of Athena of Ilion begins, and Troy VI ends: the plate has nothing to show above this line. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.label: VI G
layers.note: House VI G and its neighbours on the lower east terrace. The broad clear space between them and the wall face is Dörpfeld's ring street — “im Innern finden wir eine breite Ringstrasse, mehrere zum Centrum der Burg gerichtete Querstrassen” (1902, 2:611) — the circulation that lets defenders reach any stretch of the circuit without crossing built-up ground. It is not drawn on this plate because it is not masonry. It is the gap. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.label: Gate VI U
layers.note: The West Gate, VI U, with an opening about 2.50 m across (Tolman and Scoggin 1903). During the life of Troy VI it was walled up: Dörpfeld draws the blocking across the passage in hatching, so the defenders closed their own gate — the sort of fact a plan records and a poem does not. Nothing is drawn here but the name. A gate is a gap in the masonry, and masonry is what this plate traces.

layers.label: Gate VI T
layers.note: The South Gate, VI T — 3.20 to 3.35 m broad, its roadway paved and carrying a drainage channel half a metre deep and 0.30 to 0.40 m wide (Tolman and Scoggin 1903), flanked by tower VI i. Dörpfeld took it for the main gate: “das Hauptthor der VI. Burg ist wahrscheinlich das Süd-Thor VI T gewesen”, and identified it with Homer's Dardanian Gates, on the reasoning that Dardania lay toward Ida in the south-east — “ich ohne Zögern das Thor VI T als das dardanische bezeichnet ... habe” (1902, 2:630). The identification is his reading of the poem against the ground, not a find: no gate at Hisarlık has been shown to be a gate Homer names. Hector keeps breaking for the Dardanian Gates during the chase, hoping to get in under the well-built towers (Il. 22.194-95).

layers.label: Gate VI S
layers.note: The East Gate, VI S — a passage about 2 m wide and a door only about 1.80 m broad (Tolman and Scoggin 1903), reached along the corridor between the wall and the outer arm drawn beside it, with steps and a ramp carrying the way up inside. Dörpfeld sections it at his Fig. 41, “das Ost-Thor in der VI. Schicht (VI S) und in der VII. Schicht (VII S)”. He allowed that Homer's Scaean Gate “kann ... weiter östlich gelegen haben und würde dann vielleicht mit dem Nordost-Thor zusammenfallen” (1902, 2:630) — might have lain further east and coincided with the north-east gate. Allowed, not shown.

layers.label: Tower VI h
layers.note: The great east tower, VI h: over 11 m broad, jutting 8 m beyond the wall face, its front wall about 3 m thick, its upper storey carried on a wooden platform (Tolman and Scoggin 1903). Its footprint is drawn as part of the wall band, because that is how it stands on Dörpfeld's plate; only the name is set here.

layers.note: The south tower, VI i, beside the main gate: front wall 4.40 m broad, side walls 2.20 m thick (Tolman and Scoggin 1903), with a chamber inside it that the plate shows as a void. Whoever came up to the South Gate came up under it.

layers.label: VI A
layers.note: House VI A, built against the inner face of the west wall — a hall with an antechamber, on the megaron plan that runs through the Troy VI houses. Its masonry is drawn with the wall layer here because Dörpfeld draws the two as one mass: the house's west wall and the citadel's inner face are the same line on his sheet, and no seam is invented to part them.

layers.label: Pergamos
layers.note: The summit — and an absence, not a find. Homer's Pergamos is the top of the citadel. Apollo's temple stands Περγάμῳ εἰν ἱερῇ (Il. 5.446); he and Ares look down from it on the fighting (4.508, 7.21); Paris comes striding down from Περγάμου ἄκρης (6.512); Cassandra climbs it and is the first to see Hector's body coming home (24.700). The temple of Athena ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ that the Trojan women go up to with the robe belongs here (6.88, 6.297), and so do the houses of Priam and of Hector (6.317). Of all of it there is nothing to plan: the Hellenistic and Roman levelling for the precinct of Athena of Ilion cut the top off the mound and took Troy VI's summit with it. The part of Troy the Iliad names most often is the part the excavation cannot reach. No outline is drawn here, only the name, over the ground where it stood.

layers.label: the north side is gone
layers.note: Dörpfeld would not draw this, and neither will we. “Den ganzen nördlichen und nordwestlichen Teil der Burgmauer, von dem keine Spur erhalten ist, habe ich deshalb auch nicht einmal durch punktirte Linien anzudeuten gewagt” (1902, 2:650): of the whole northern and north-western part of the citadel wall, of which no trace survives, he did not dare even to suggest the line with dots. He restored it elsewhere, on the small conjectural plan at his Fig. 470, where he marked what was unsecured with dotting and question marks, and he kept the survey plan clean. The gap between the wall's two broken ends is not a defect in this drawing. It is the state of the evidence — and it is exactly where the poem's traffic runs, out through the Scaean Gate πεδίον δέ, toward the plain and the ships. There must have been a gate on this side. Nothing of it is left. Dörpfeld put the Scaean Gate at the north-west corner vermutungsweise, by conjecture, and admitted at once that it “auch weiter östlich gelegen haben kann”, might equally have lain further east. No point is marked for it on this plate, because there is no coordinate to mark.
